title: Morphisms Local Rings and Rational Maps of Affine Varieties

items.title: Regular functions on open subsets of a classical affine variety
Regular functions on a classical affine variety form a sheaf
items.strategy: Refine to a principal-open cover using the affine basis from AV-1. Uniqueness is pointwise because regular functions are honest functions, and existence follows by comparing the local fractions in the principal localizations and clearing denominators against a finite unit-ideal decomposition.

items.title: Global regular functions on a classical affine variety are its coordinate ring
items.strategy: Cover the affine variety by finitely many principal opens on which the given regular function is a quotient g_i / s_i^{n_i}. After raising to a common exponent and using that the s_i generate the unit ideal, the standard sum-of-one argument rewrites the global function as a single element of the coordinate ring.

items.title: Morphisms of classical affine varieties
Images and fibres of a regular map
Affine morphisms are contravariantly equivalent to coordinate-ring homomorphisms
items.strategy: A morphism pulls back every global regular function on the target, and the global-regular-functions theorem identifies the pullback ring with the source coordinate ring. Conversely, a k-algebra homomorphism provides coordinate functions on the source; the defining equations of the target show that those functions land in the target, and identities and composition are literal pullback identities.

items.title: The affine algebraic-set dictionary is contravariantly full and faithful on classical affine varieties
items.strategy: AV-1 already supplies the object-side correspondence between affine algebraic sets and reduced affine k-algebras. The classical affine morphism theorem then shows that on the classical affine-variety subcategory the coordinate-ring assignment is contravariantly full and faithful.

items.title: Morphisms from an irreducible affine variety to an affine variety are determined by a dense open subset
items.strategy: Embed the target affine variety in affine space and compose the two morphisms with the coordinate functions. Each coordinate difference is a global regular function on the source that vanishes on a dense open subset, so its zero locus is a closed set containing a dense subset and therefore all of the source.

items.title: Germs of regular functions and the local ring at a point of a classical affine variety
The local ring at a point of an affine variety is the localization at its maximal ideal
items.strategy: Send a germ represented near x by g / h to the fraction g / h in the localization at the maximal ideal m_x. Principal-open neighborhoods around x make this map well defined, and every localization fraction has a representative regular on some principal open containing x, giving the inverse construction.

items.title: The residue field at a classical point
Affine open subsets of a classical affine variety
The function field of an irreducible classical affine variety
All nonempty affine opens of an irreducible affine variety have the same function field
items.strategy: A nonempty affine open contains a nonempty principal open. Applying the principal-open localization theorem inside both the ambient variety and the affine open identifies the two coordinate rings after inverting one nonzero function, and localizing a domain at a nonzero element does not change its field of fractions.

items.title: A rational function is regular at a point exactly when it lies in the local ring
Rational maps between irreducible classical affine varieties
The rational-map equivalence relation is transitive
items.strategy: If two representatives agree on one nonempty open set and the second pair agrees on another, then both agreements hold on the intersection with the middle domain. Irreducibility makes every nonempty open subset dense, so the intersection is still nonempty and gives the common witness required for transitivity.

items.title: The maximal domain of definition of a rational map to an affine variety
Dominant morphisms and dominant rational maps
Dominant maps pull back function fields functorially
items.strategy: Represent a rational function on the target by a regular function on a nonempty affine open and pull it back along a dominant representative. Shrinking to smaller common affine opens proves independence of all choices, and composition is literal pullback of representatives on the common domain where both composites are defined.

items.title: Dominant rational maps to an affine variety correspond to injective homomorphisms of function fields
items.strategy: A dominant rational map defines a nonzero k-algebra map on the target function field by pullback, hence an injection. Conversely, after choosing an affine chart on the source where the images of finitely many coordinate generators become regular, the affine morphism theorem produces a representative morphism on a nonempty affine open, and shrinking the target if needed makes the construction independent of the chosen generators.

items.title: Birational maps and birational equivalence of classical affine varieties
Irreducible affine varieties are birational exactly when their function fields are isomorphic
items.strategy: A birational inverse yields mutually inverse pullback maps on function fields. Conversely, an isomorphism of function fields gives dominant rational maps both ways by the correspondence theorem, and the induced pullbacks compose to the identity, so the two rational maps are inverse in the birational sense.

title: Morphisms Local Rings and Rational Maps of Affine Varieties — Examples

items.title: A polynomial map and its pullback on coordinate rings
items.strategy: Use the map (s,t) mapsto (s,s^2,t) from affine space to the surface y - x^2 = 0, compute the induced pullback on the coordinate classes x, y, z, and verify that every defining relation of the target vanishes after substitution.

items.title: The hyperbola xy = 1 is isomorphic to the punctured affine line
items.strategy: Map t to (t,t^{-1}) and project back to the first coordinate. The punctured affine line already has Laurent-polynomial coordinate ring, so the affine morphism theorem identifies the inverse pullbacks and proves that the two maps are inverse isomorphisms.

items.title: When char(k) is not 2, the affine circle x^2 + y^2 = 1 is birational to the affine line
items.strategy: Use the line of slope t through the point (-1,0). Its second intersection with the circle is ((1 - t^2)/(1 + t^2), 2t/(1 + t^2)), and on the dense open where x != -1 the inverse rational parameter is t = y/(x + 1).

items.title: The rational map (x,y) mapsto y / x on the affine plane is undefined along x = 0
items.strategy: Regard y / x as a regular function on the principal open D(x), hence as a rational map to A^1. If it extended regularly across a point of x = 0, shrink to a principal-open neighbourhood and compare the extension with y / x inside the localized coordinate ring there; clearing denominators then forces an impossible identity at the point with x = 0 and y != 0.

items.title: The affine line and its punctured principal open are birational but not isomorphic
items.strategy: The identity on the common dense open A^1 \ {0} gives the birational equivalence. An isomorphism would induce an isomorphism of coordinate rings, but the punctured affine line has Laurent-polynomial coordinate ring while A^1 has polynomial coordinate ring, so the affine morphism theorem rules out an isomorphism.

items.title: The local ring of the affine line at the origin consists of rational functions defined at the origin
items.strategy: Identify the origin with the maximal ideal (t) in k[t], apply the local-ring localization theorem to obtain k[t]_(t), and read off its units and residue field from the published abstract-algebra computation of the same localization.

items.title: The cusp parametrization t mapsto (t^2,t^3) is bijective but not an isomorphism
items.strategy: The map from A^1 to the cusp y^2 = x^3 corresponds to the homomorphism k[u,v]/(v^2-u^3) -> k[t] with u mapsto t^2 and v mapsto t^3. That homomorphism is injective but not surjective because t is not in its image, so the affine morphism theorem rules out an isomorphism even though the point map is bijective.
